Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The laundromat on Fourth Street never locks its doors, mostly because the deadbolt rusted inside the frame three winters ago and nobody has bothered to drill it out. At two in the morning in late November, it sits on the corner like a bright, rectangular aquarium washed up in the dark. Inside, the air is ten degrees warmer than it has any right to be, heavy with the scent of artificial lavender, scorched dust, and the damp, mineral breath of wet cotton. When I push the glass door open, the bell overhead doesn’t ring—its clapper is missing—so I enter quietly, lugging a canvas sack full of everything I own that has begun to smell like stagnation.

There is a specific kind of amnesty granted to anyone awake between two and four. The daytime rules of efficiency and posture dissolve. Nobody asks why you are washing your bedsheets while the rest of the zip code is dreaming. In the far corner, beneath a faded poster explaining how to treat grass stains, a woman in pale blue scrubs sits on the folding table, her knees drawn to her chest, staring at nothing with the hollowed-out calm of someone who has spent twelve hours on linoleum floors. Three machines down, an older man in a wool overcoat reads a paperback whose cover has been torn off. Every few minutes, he licks his thumb, turns a page, and checks the silver watch on his wrist, as if waiting for a train that only stops here.

I feed quarters into Washer Six. They drop through the metal slide with a heavy, satisfying clunk, a mechanical agreement that for the next twenty-eight minutes, something in my life will be handled properly. When the water rushes in, it hisses like surf pulling back over gravel. I pour the detergent—too much, always too much—and watch the suds bloom against the circular glass. Behind the porthole, my shirts and socks lose their identities. They stop being the things I wore to bad meetings or on long walks home; they become pure color and motion, tangling and untangling in a gray soup. There is a quiet hypnosis in watching your own debris get tumbled into submission. For a little while, the machine does the work of forgetting for you.

I don’t have a good reason for being awake. Nothing terrible happened today, and nothing terrible is scheduled for tomorrow. It’s just that sometime in the last month, the silence in my apartment grew too large for the furniture. I moved in September, and there are still two cardboard boxes taped shut in the hallway, labeled *Kitchen – Misc.* in black marker, sitting like monoliths to a life I haven’t quite decided to resume. When sleep won’t come, you can either lie in the dark and let your mind inventory every small mistake you made in 2018, or you can put on your coat, gather your linens, and walk four blocks through the drizzle to sit under buzzing fluorescent tubes. At least here, the noise is honest. The machines groan, the change dispenser hums, and somewhere in the back a single sneaker thumps against a dryer drum like a steady, unhurried heart.

The lint traps are the strangest part of this place. Before I transfer my load to Dryer Four, I pull out the mesh screen and peel away a thick, gray sheet of felt. It always strikes me as faintly intimate, holding the microscopic cast-offs of strangers—threads from a child’s sweater, a mechanic’s overalls, a bartender’s apron, all spun together into one soft, uniform dust. Everything we wear is slowly coming apart, fiber by fiber, and this is where the evidence collects. I drop the gray cloud into the trash, toss in my damp clothes, and push the button marked *High*. The drum catches with a shudder, and the warm breath of the vent hits my shins. Outside, a delivery truck hisses past, its headlights sweeping across the wall and turning the rain on the window into brief, bright streaks of silver.

While the dryer spins, I sit in a bolted-down orange plastic chair and watch our reflections in the front glass. Beside the vending machine, the woman in scrubs has leaned her temple against the cool metal. Her eyes are closed, though I don’t think she is sleeping; she is just letting the machinery idle.

Twenty minutes later, the old man’s buzzer goes off—a harsh, metallic bray that makes the woman blink herself back into the room. He stands, tucks his coverless book into his coat pocket, and begins folding his clothes with astonishing, ceremonial precision. Every collar is smoothed, every cuff aligned, every crease pressed flat with the heel of his palm. Watching him, I feel a sudden, inexplicable gratitude for people who still take care with small things when nobody is looking. When he finishes, he lifts his basket, nods once to the woman and once to me—a brief salute between citizens of the night shift—and steps out into the rain. The door swings shut behind him with a hydraulic sigh.

My own cycle ends at 3:30. When I open the dryer door, the heat rolls out in a wave that smells of clean cotton and mild static. I bury my face in a bath towel for two seconds longer than necessary, drinking in the ridiculous, temporary luxury of something warm. I don’t fold anything as neatly as the old man did; I just bundle the hot clothes into my canvas bag, sling it over my shoulder, and step back into the dark. The rain has thinned to a cold mist. The street is empty, the city is still asleep, and pressed against my ribs, I am carrying a small, fading furnace all the way home.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective first-person night scene uses the laundromat and its strangers to give shape to loneliness and temporary comfort.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, sensuous, and quietly lonely, attentive to smells, sounds, worn objects, and small gestures. Its pathos comes less from a stated crisis than from the silence of the apartment, the unopened moving boxes, and the narrator’s need to be somewhere the noise feels “honest.” The older man’s careful folding and the brief nods between night visitors offer a modest kind of human recognition. The reader is invited to find dignity and relief in ordinary maintenance, without pretending that a warm towel solves what waits at home.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds a broken deadbolt, fluorescent light, wet clothes, lint, and the night-shift strangers sharing the laundromat. Washing becomes both a mechanical reprieve from rumination and an image of how lives shed pieces over time; warmth and small acts of care provide the scene’s understated consolation.

## Evidence line
> For a little while, the machine does the work of forgetting for you.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained sensory detail and recurring movement between decay, care, and temporary warmth make this a distinctive, coherent expression.
